report:
**Conclusion:** The best current evidence does **not** show that ivermectin lowers the risk of death from COVID-19.

Why: early small studies and meta-analyses sometimes reported benefit, but they were vulnerable to bias, inconsistent methods, very few deaths, and—in parts of the early ivermectin literature—serious data-quality concerns. Such findings are hypothesis-generating, not reliable proof of a mortality benefit.

More informative are larger, randomized, placebo-controlled trials. The Brazilian TOGETHER platform trial tested early ivermectin in higher-risk outpatients and found no clinically meaningful reduction in COVID-19 progression (hospital observation/admission); deaths were too uncommon to establish a mortality benefit. Later large placebo-controlled trials also failed to show meaningful clinical benefit, including at a higher dose. A 2024 systematic review summarized that ivermectin did not reduce in-hospital mortality, ICU use, ventilation, or disease severity.

It is important to distinguish “no demonstrated benefit” from proof that it can *never* help any narrowly defined group: no trial can prove an effect is exactly zero. But the accumulated randomized evidence provides no credible basis to prescribe ivermectin to reduce COVID-19 deaths. It is not FDA-approved for COVID-19; animal formulations and excessive doses can cause serious toxicity. For an individual case, use evidence-based COVID-19 treatment guidance from a clinician, especially for people at high risk.
